items.title: A Brief History of Intelligence
items.author: Max Bennett
items.summary:
Max Bennett's *A Brief History of Intelligence* investigates how biological evolution produced the extraordinary cognitive capacities of the human mind and what that history might reveal about artificial intelligence. His central argument is that intelligence emerged through five cumulative evolutionary breakthroughs: steering, reinforcing, simulating, mentalizing and speaking. Each breakthrough built upon earlier neural machinery, progressively expanding what organisms could perceive, learn, imagine and communicate.

The first breakthrough, **steering**, emerged in early bilaterally organised animals. Nervous systems developed the capacity to integrate sensory information, distinguish beneficial from harmful stimuli and coordinate movement accordingly. Rather than responding through isolated reflexes, organisms could make integrated choices about approaching opportunities and avoiding threats. This established the foundations of purposeful behaviour, including the valuation mechanisms upon which later learning systems would depend.

The second breakthrough, **reinforcing**, enabled animals to learn through trial and error. Bennett draws connections between vertebrate neural structures and reinforcement-learning concepts. The basal ganglia support action selection, while dopamine signalling resembles the prediction-error mechanisms through which learning systems update expectations about future rewards. The developing cortex and associated structures supported increasingly sophisticated representations of patterns, time and space. Animals could consequently learn which actions worked, under what circumstances and with what expected consequences.

The third breakthrough, **simulating**, transformed intelligence by allowing organisms to evaluate possibilities before acting. Bennett associates this development with expanding mammalian cortical capabilities. Internal representations of the world and potential actions made it possible to imagine alternative outcomes, plan behaviour and learn from hypothetical scenarios. Intelligence was no longer restricted to direct experience. This distinction resembles the difference between model-free reinforcement learning, which learns from experienced outcomes, and model-based learning, which evaluates potential actions through an internal model.

The fourth breakthrough, **mentalizing**, extended simulation toward the representation of mental states. Bennett proposes that primate cognitive development made possible more sophisticated models of one's own mind and, through related mechanisms, the intentions and knowledge of other individuals. These capabilities support theory of mind, imitation learning and anticipation of future needs. His account of mentalizing as a higher-order generative model is a theoretical proposal supported by converging evidence, rather than an established neuroscientific explanation.

The fifth breakthrough, **speaking**, enabled intelligence to extend beyond individual brains. Language supported increasingly sophisticated cooperation, instruction and cultural transmission. Bennett connects its development to interacting ecological, technological and social pressures, including tool-making and expanding cooperative relationships. Knowledge could now accumulate across individuals and generations, producing cultural capabilities far exceeding those of any isolated human.

Bennett's framework also provides a perspective on contemporary AI. Artificial systems display impressive abilities in some cognitive domains while struggling with others that biological evolution developed much earlier. Reconstructing the dependencies among evolutionary breakthroughs may therefore illuminate missing or incomplete artificial capabilities.

He speculates that artificial superintelligence could represent a sixth breakthrough, potentially escaping biological constraints on processing speed, energy and reproduction. This remains a forward-looking possibility, distinct from his evolutionary reconstruction.

**The central conclusion:** Human intelligence is a layered evolutionary achievement. Understanding how its capabilities accumulated offers a framework for investigating both biological cognition and the future development of AI.

items.title: AI Engineering
items.author: Chip Huyen
items.summary:
Chip Huyen's *AI Engineering: Building Applications with Foundation Models* explains how to convert powerful general-purpose AI models into useful, reliable and economically sustainable applications. Its central argument is that foundation models have changed the engineering problem. Developers increasingly begin with pretrained models rather than constructing task-specific machine-learning systems from scratch. The difficult work shifts toward evaluating, adapting, integrating and operating these models within complete applications.

Huyen begins with a critical distinction between an impressive demonstration and a production-ready system. Foundation models make prototypes relatively easy to build, but practical deployment requires much more than convincing outputs. Developers must establish whether AI is appropriate for the business problem, determine acceptable performance, choose between building and buying, and identify where human involvement remains necessary. Reliability, security, latency and cost all influence whether an application is genuinely useful.

**Evaluation is central to the engineering process.** Foundation models produce open-ended, probabilistic outputs, making correctness difficult to measure through conventional automated tests alone. Huyen distinguishes functional evaluation, human judgment, comparative testing and AI-assisted evaluation. Public benchmarks can help compare models but rarely capture the specific requirements of a production application. Developers therefore need application-specific evaluation pipelines that measure factuality, task performance, safety, responsiveness and operating cost. AI judges can supplement this process, although their own inconsistency and potential biases require independent checks.

The book identifies several ways to adapt foundation-model behaviour. Prompt engineering modifies instructions, examples and output specifications. Context construction supplies relevant information at inference time. Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, retrieves external material and incorporates it into the model's context, improving access to application-specific or current knowledge. Agentic systems extend capabilities through planning, tool use and repeated interaction with the environment. These additions create new failure modes, especially when models can access sensitive information or perform consequential actions.

Finetuning provides a different intervention by modifying model weights. It can improve specialised behaviour, formats and task performance, but requires suitable data and additional resources. Parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA reduce training costs. Huyen distinguishes adapting behaviour through weights from supplying information through retrieval, while emphasising that the approaches can complement one another.

Dataset engineering consequently becomes an important discipline. Data must have appropriate quality, coverage and quantity. Annotation, cleaning, deduplication and synthetic-data generation can support improvement, but generated examples still require verification. The quality of training and evaluation data ultimately constrains system performance.

Inference engineering addresses the economics of deployment. Developers must manage latency, throughput, memory utilisation and cost through techniques including batching, caching, quantisation and distillation. An accurate model that is too slow or expensive may still be unsuitable.

Finally, Huyen treats AI applications as integrated systems involving context management, guardrails, model routing, observability and feedback. Production monitoring should expose failures and generate evidence for subsequent improvements. User feedback is valuable but potentially biased and must be interpreted carefully.

**The central conclusion:** Successful AI engineering depends on disciplined system development. Start with the application, establish evaluation, adopt the simplest effective adaptation, optimise operational trade-offs and improve continuously through measured feedback.

items.title: Atlas of AI
items.author: Kate Crawford
items.summary:
Kate Crawford's *Atlas of AI* challenges the conventional portrayal of artificial intelligence as an abstract technological achievement. Her central argument is that AI is fundamentally a material, political and institutional system. Its apparent computational autonomy conceals enormous dependencies on natural resources, human labour, appropriated data, classificatory practices and concentrated corporate and state power.

Crawford begins by examining the **physical foundations of AI**. Computational infrastructure depends on mining, energy production, water, manufacturing and extensive logistical networks. The seemingly immaterial cloud requires substantial extraction from the Earth. Her investigation of lithium mining and the environmental costs of computational infrastructure shows how digital innovation creates physical consequences frequently omitted from technological narratives.

The second dimension concerns labour. AI systems depend on workers across mining, logistics, manufacturing, data annotation, software development and platform operations. Automation often reorganises and obscures labour rather than eliminating it. Crawford's discussion of Amazon fulfilment centres illustrates how algorithmic management can intensify surveillance, standardise productivity expectations and increase managerial control over human activity. The apparent independence of automated systems therefore relies on extensive human work.

The third dimension is data extraction. Crawford argues that training data is actively collected, selected, organised and repurposed rather than simply discovered. Images, behaviour, public records and online information become inputs into commercial systems. Her discussion of biometric datasets and disputes involving health information highlights questions of consent, ownership and the conversion of shared informational resources into privately controlled assets.

**Classification is a particularly important mechanism.** Machine-learning systems require complex social reality to be translated into measurable categories. Those classifications inevitably simplify, prioritise and exclude aspects of the world. Crawford traces connections between historical measurement practices and contemporary machine-learning datasets to demonstrate that classification has political consequences. Categories influence who becomes visible, how people are compared and which institutional judgments appear legitimate.

Her examination of emotion-recognition technology provides a powerful example. Systems that claim to infer internal emotions from facial expressions often rely on scientifically contested assumptions about universal emotional categories. Improving technical accuracy cannot necessarily resolve an invalid underlying premise. Yet such systems have been promoted for hiring, education, policing and security.

The final dimension concerns state power. AI has developed through relationships involving military institutions, intelligence agencies, police organisations and private technology companies. Surveillance infrastructures and predictive systems extend the capacity of institutions to observe, classify and intervene in social life. Corporate capabilities increasingly support state objectives while states become dependent on private technological infrastructure.

Crawford integrates these dimensions through the concept of AI as a **registry of power**. Material extraction, labour relations, datasets and classifications reflect the priorities of institutions capable of financing, designing and deploying computational systems. Benefits and costs are distributed unequally.

Her conclusion extends beyond improving algorithmic fairness. Meaningful responses may require labour protection, environmental accountability, restrictions on surveillance and political refusal of applications whose purposes are themselves objectionable.

**The central conclusion:** Understanding AI requires examining the complete systems of extraction and power that make it possible. The fundamental questions concern who controls AI, whose interests it serves and who bears its consequences.

items.title: Being
items.author: Menzies & Menzies
items.summary:
*Being* examines the psychological and existential difficulties that arise from human consciousness. Rachel and Ross Menzies argue that many forms of suffering emerge from the very capacities that distinguish human experience: self-awareness, imagination, memory, anticipation, attachment and knowledge of mortality. These abilities make meaningful living possible while simultaneously exposing people to anxiety, isolation, uncertainty, regret and loss.

The authors' organising insight is that the fundamental problems of existence cannot be permanently solved or escaped. Human beings cannot guarantee certainty, eliminate vulnerability, avoid loss or overcome mortality. Attempts to secure impossible control frequently increase suffering. A more fulfilling life becomes possible through understanding these conditions, accepting their limits and deliberately organising one's choices around meaningful values and relationships.

One recurring difficulty is the **inner voice**. Human thought continually remembers, predicts, evaluates and criticises. Memories generate regret, imagined possibilities produce anxiety, and self-reflection can become harsh self-judgment. The authors argue that people often give this internal commentary unwarranted authority. Psychological flexibility involves learning to notice thoughts without automatically treating them as facts or instructions.

Self-awareness also produces existential isolation. However closely individuals connect, they cannot completely experience another person's consciousness. Moreover, identity is partly shaped by family history, cultural expectations and social relationships. The resulting challenge is to distinguish inherited assumptions from personally chosen values. Authenticity develops through deliberate, values-consistent action rather than the discovery of an entirely independent or fixed self.

Family relationships are especially consequential. Attachment patterns, expectations and emotional responses can pass between generations. The authors resist simplistic parental blame, recognising that parents themselves inherit influences from earlier relationships. These patterns are nevertheless malleable, and new connections can reshape established ways of relating.

Love and belonging provide important resources for navigating existence. Social connection supports psychological and physical wellbeing, while isolation creates vulnerabilities. The authors discuss research concerning relationships, group membership and social prescribing to demonstrate why connection matters beyond its immediate emotional rewards.

Meaning and hope provide another response to existential uncertainty. Life does not arrive with guaranteed meaning, but individuals can construct purpose through relationships, chosen commitments, contribution and valued activities. Religious belief can offer belonging, direction and consolation, although the authors also examine its potential to generate guilt, judgment and fear. Faith is therefore treated as a possible response to existential difficulties rather than a universal solution.

The book ultimately confronts impermanence, grief, choice and death. Loss is unavoidable, and anticipation can make people suffer before the feared event occurs. The authors consider the psychological consequences of deterministic views of behaviour, including their potential to reduce blame, shame and regret.

Across these themes, acceptance emerges as the integrating response. Acceptance means acknowledging unavoidable realities while continuing to act meaningfully. It does not eliminate grief, anxiety or mortality; it changes how people organise their lives around these conditions.

**The central conclusion:** Human existence contains unavoidable uncertainty, separation and loss. Understanding and accepting these limits creates room for authentic values, sustaining relationships, meaningful commitments and a more deliberate use of finite time.

items.title: Beyond the Second Brain
items.author: GP
items.summary:
*Beyond the Second Brain* examines a growing problem in personal knowledge management: the widening gap between information stored in external systems and knowledge that has become genuinely usable by the individual. Its central argument is that organising information is a different achievement from developing understanding. Generative AI makes this distinction especially important because it can now perform many of the cognitive activities traditionally involved in learning.

Personal knowledge systems have developed powerful methods for capturing, organising, linking and retrieving information. Zettelkasten, evergreen notes, PARA, digital notebooks and AI-assisted search all address genuine limitations of memory and information management. Yet a perfectly organised knowledge library does not guarantee that its owner can reconstruct an argument, recognise a faulty explanation or apply a framework to an unfamiliar problem.

The essay distinguishes **information availability, externally organised knowledge and internally usable knowledge**. Only the third constitutes capability possessed by the person. External systems can support thinking, but the individual must still interpret answers, assess evidence, identify omissions and exercise judgment.

Generative AI introduces an efficiency paradox. It removes friction from summarising, comparing, explaining and mapping ideas. Some of this effort is genuinely wasteful. Other forms of effort are precisely how understanding develops. When AI completes intellectually productive tasks before the learner engages with them, the resulting artefacts may be excellent while the learner's capabilities remain unchanged.

The essay draws on the concept of mental schemas to explain expertise. Experts organise information into meaningful, conditional patterns that allow them to interpret situations efficiently. A finance professional, for example, can connect falling revenue, declining utilisation and deteriorating margins into a coherent explanation of unused capacity. This capability depends on organised internal knowledge rather than simply recalling isolated facts.

Visual knowledge maps can help externalise these schemas. However, viewing a familiar map creates a risk of confusing recognition with mastery. The essay distinguishes recognition, recall and transfer. Recognising a concept when prompted is easier than reconstructing it unaided, while applying it to an unfamiliar situation demands deeper understanding.

**Productive friction** is therefore central to the proposed learning approach. Extraneous difficulty should be removed, while useful cognitive effort should be preserved. Retrieval practice, reconstruction, comparison, counterexamples and application exercises make learning more demanding because they strengthen capability.

The essay also proposes differentiated learning depths. Some material needs only to remain available for reference. Other knowledge deserves recognition, working understanding, operational mastery or integration into one's core intellectual architecture. This prevents personal knowledge systems from accumulating material without intellectual prioritisation.

AI can support this process through deliberately assigned roles: examiner, diagnostician, challenger, transfer coach, integrator and calibration partner. Instead of always supplying immediate answers, it can require learners to reconstruct ideas, expose weaknesses and defend applications under unfamiliar conditions.

The proposed practice moves through source engagement, structural externalisation, retrieval, connection, transfer, challenge, calibration and integration. Over time, knowledge from separate sources becomes part of the learner's own conceptual architecture.

**The central conclusion:** The ultimate measure of a knowledge system is the intellectual development of its user. AI should remove unproductive effort while preserving the thinking necessary to build durable understanding, transferable expertise and calibrated judgment.

items.title: Careless People
items.author: Sarah Wynn-Williams
items.summary:
Sarah Wynn-Williams's *Careless People* is a memoir of her years inside Facebook, tracing the company's development from an idealistic technology organisation into a global institution possessing enormous political and social influence. Her central contention is that Facebook's growth, wealth and power expanded much faster than its capacity or willingness to exercise responsibility.

Wynn-Williams joined Facebook because she believed digital connectivity could strengthen civic participation, help communities coordinate and change the relationship between individuals and political institutions. Her earlier diplomatic experience led her to recognise that Facebook was becoming an important geopolitical actor. The platform's usefulness during emergencies, including the Christchurch earthquake, reinforced her belief that it could serve as an unprecedented form of civic infrastructure.

However, the company's operational priorities increasingly diverged from its public mission. **Growth became the dominant institutional incentive.** Expanding user numbers, entering new markets and removing barriers received greater attention than developing appropriate safeguards. The pursuit of scale encouraged executives to regard political and regulatory constraints primarily as obstacles to expansion.

As Facebook became embedded in societies worldwide, it acquired influence over elections, public discourse, political mobilisation and relations with governments. Yet its internal governance remained improvisational. Wynn-Williams recounts how leaders initially showed limited understanding of the political consequences of their platform, even as heads of government began treating the company as a major international actor.

Myanmar illustrates the danger of this mismatch. Facebook's growing reach coincided with serious ethnic and religious tensions, while concerns about misinformation and hate speech were inadequately addressed. The company's largely standardised technological approach struggled to accommodate complex local political and cultural conditions.

The pursuit of access to China provides another major test. Wynn-Williams describes how commercial ambitions created pressure to accommodate the demands of an authoritarian government. The episode exposes tensions between Facebook's stated commitments to openness and its willingness to compromise principles when substantial market opportunities were involved.

The 2016 US presidential election further demonstrated that Facebook had become political infrastructure. Its influence over information distribution and political mobilisation made claims of platform neutrality increasingly difficult to sustain. In the aftermath, employees confronted questions about the company's role in democratic processes and the responsibilities arising from its technological power.

Wynn-Williams also describes internal organisational failures. Concentrated executive authority, loyalty expectations and the difficulty of communicating uncomfortable truths weakened accountability. Her account includes allegations concerning workplace harassment and gender discrimination, which should be understood as claims made in her memoir. These experiences parallel her broader criticism: powerful individuals and institutions can become insulated from consequences.

The recurring institutional mechanism is a cycle in which idealism legitimises expansion, expansion creates power, power insulates decision-makers, and weakened accountability allows harmful behaviour to persist.

The memoir concludes by connecting Facebook's history to Meta's expanding involvement in artificial intelligence. Wynn-Williams argues that the organisational habits established during the social-media era remain relevant as the potential consequences of technological decisions become more substantial.

**The central conclusion:** Extraordinary technological power becomes dangerous when institutional incentives reward expansion while insulating leaders from accountability. Facebook's history illustrates the consequences of allowing private influence over society to grow faster than responsible governance.

items.title: Change: How to Make Big Things Happen
items.author: Damon Centola
items.summary:
Damon Centola's *Change* challenges conventional assumptions about how innovations, behaviours and social movements spread. His central argument is that significant social change usually depends on repeated reinforcement within social networks rather than the rapid dissemination of information.

Conventional diffusion strategies emphasise influential individuals, viral transmission and highly attractive ideas. Centola argues that these approaches often confuse awareness with adoption. A message may reach millions of people without changing their behaviour, particularly when adoption involves uncertainty, social risk or coordination with others.

The book's foundational distinction is between **simple contagion and complex contagion**. Simple contagions, including many forms of information transmission, can spread through a single exposure. Weak social ties are effective because they carry information across otherwise disconnected communities. Complex contagions operate differently. People contemplating unfamiliar or risky behaviours often require reinforcement from several relevant individuals before acting.

Centola identifies four important barriers to adoption: coordination, credibility, legitimacy and excitement. People need to know whether others will participate, whether an innovation works, whether their social environment will approve and whether a movement is gaining momentum. Multiple reinforcing relationships can overcome these barriers.

Network structure consequently becomes decisive. Centola contrasts widely dispersed, weakly connected networks with clustered networks containing overlapping social relationships. His Health-Buddy experiment demonstrates that information can travel faster through dispersed networks while actual behavioural adoption is greater and more persistent in clustered networks.

This finding changes the meaning of redundancy. In information transmission, repeated exposure may appear wasteful. In behavioural change, redundancy supplies trust, evidence and social reinforcement.

The book develops practical implications for network design. Innovations can gain an initial foothold within relatively protected peripheral communities, where established norms exert less countervailing pressure. Once local adoption becomes established, change can spread through **wide bridges** consisting of multiple reinforcing relationships between communities. A single connection may communicate an idea, but several connections are often needed to make adoption socially credible.

Reinforcement also depends on who provides it. Similar individuals may strengthen credibility and emotional identification. Diverse social contacts can demonstrate that a new behaviour enjoys broad legitimacy. The appropriate network structure therefore depends on the particular barrier to change.

Centola's research on social conventions identifies an experimental tipping point around 25% committed participation under specified coordination conditions. The result illustrates how a sufficiently organised minority can alter collective expectations and trigger broader adoption. It is not a universal threshold applicable to every social movement.

His recommended strategy resembles a snowball: establish a reinforcing cluster, protect early adopters, build connections across communities and expand toward critical mass.

The argument ultimately extends beyond diffusion. Networks influence which ideas are heard, which perspectives are suppressed and how groups collectively reason. More egalitarian structures can help preserve diverse information and improve collective discovery. Yet cross-group connections alone may fail to reduce polarisation when divisive identities remain salient.

**The central conclusion:** Durable social change depends on the architecture of relationships. Successful changemakers build networks that provide sufficient reinforcement for unfamiliar behaviours to acquire credibility, legitimacy and eventually the status of a new social norm.

items.title: Chokepoints
items.author: Edward Fishman
items.summary:
Edward Fishman's *Chokepoints* examines how the United States transformed global economic interdependence into an increasingly sophisticated instrument of geopolitical coercion. His central argument is that globalisation created concentrated dependencies within finance, technology and supply chains. Control over these critical nodes gave Washington and its allies extraordinary economic power, but repeated weaponisation is encouraging other countries to reduce the very dependencies that make such power possible.

The book begins with a structural observation: international economic activity appears geographically dispersed, yet essential infrastructure is often highly concentrated. Dollar clearing, correspondent banking relationships, semiconductor design software and advanced chip-manufacturing equipment all represent potential chokepoints. States controlling access to these systems can exercise influence far beyond their territorial borders.

**Modern economic warfare operates through exclusion from indispensable networks.** Rather than relying solely on direct trade restrictions, governments can pressure third-country institutions to stop dealing with designated targets. Banks and companies become enforcement mechanisms because continued commercial relationships with sanctioned entities may threaten their own access to Western markets or infrastructure.

Fishman develops this argument through successive geopolitical campaigns.

Iran provides the foundational case for financial coercion. Facing concerns about Iran's nuclear programme, American policymakers developed sanctions that made international banks increasingly reluctant to handle Iranian transactions. Financial isolation and restrictions on oil revenues helped create pressure leading toward the 2015 nuclear agreement. However, subsequent events demonstrate that economic pressure does not guarantee durable political outcomes.

Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014 presented a different challenge. Russia's economic size, energy relationships and geopolitical importance made comprehensive economic exclusion dangerous. Western governments therefore employed more targeted restrictions against banks, individuals, financing arrangements and strategic technologies. These measures imposed costs without compelling Russia to reverse the annexation.

China demonstrated the potential of technological chokepoints. Restrictions affecting Huawei illustrated how American legal authority could extend into foreign-manufactured products dependent on US technology. The semiconductor ecosystem became a strategic instrument because essential capabilities were concentrated across the United States and allied economies. These restrictions also intensified China's determination to develop alternative technological capabilities.

Following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Western governments combined financial sanctions, immobilisation of central-bank reserves, export controls and restrictions involving energy services. The campaign demonstrated the breadth of the economic arsenal while revealing its limitations. Russia suffered significant costs but avoided immediate economic collapse, and sanctions did not independently secure Western strategic objectives.

Fishman therefore distinguishes **economic damage from political success**. Effective coercion requires clear objectives, allied coordination, credible threats and an understanding of the costs imposed on both the target and the coalition.

The book's deeper argument concerns systemic consequences. Once countries recognise economic dependencies as strategic vulnerabilities, they pursue self-sufficiency, alternative financial networks, diversified supply chains and industrial policies.

Fishman frames the resulting dilemma through an impossible trinity involving economic interdependence, economic security and geopolitical competition. Sustaining all three becomes increasingly difficult. Continued geopolitical rivalry is therefore likely to weaken aspects of global economic integration.

**The central conclusion:** Globalisation gave the United States powerful economic weapons by concentrating essential infrastructure within networks it could influence. The use of those weapons is encouraging fragmentation, potentially weakening economic coercion as an alternative to direct military confrontation.

items.title: Co-Intelligence
items.author: Ethan Mollick
items.summary:
Ethan Mollick's *Co-Intelligence* explores how people should work, learn and create alongside increasingly capable generative AI. His central argument is that AI already possesses sufficient cognitive capability to transform many human activities, yet remains unpredictable, uneven and unreliable. Effective collaboration therefore requires extensive experimentation combined with human expertise, responsibility and judgment.

Mollick proposes treating AI as a form of co-intelligence: a flexible, nonhuman collaborator capable of contributing to numerous intellectual tasks. This framing differs from conventional software because generative AI produces probabilistic responses rather than merely executing predictable instructions. Its outputs can be creative, insightful and useful while also containing convincing errors.

A central concept is the **Jagged Frontier** of AI capability. Models may perform extraordinarily well on tasks that appear difficult while failing at apparently simpler activities. The boundary between competence and failure is difficult to identify in advance and changes as technology develops.

Mollick illustrates this problem through research involving Boston Consulting Group consultants. AI assistance improved performance on tasks within the technology's capabilities, but participants became less accurate on a deliberately selected task outside that frontier. The evidence demonstrates that apparent fluency can encourage excessive trust.

The book introduces four practical rules for using AI.

First, always invite AI to the table. Experimenting broadly helps discover useful applications and identify emerging capabilities. Second, remain the human in the loop. AI outputs require verification, contextual interpretation and accountability. Third, treat AI like a person while specifying what kind of person it should simulate. Assigning roles and perspectives can improve interaction, provided users remember that humanlike behaviour does not establish personhood. Fourth, assume that current AI is the least capable version one will encounter. Working methods should anticipate continuing technological development.

Mollick distinguishes two approaches to collaboration. In the **Centaur model**, humans and AI divide tasks according to comparative strengths. In the **Cyborg model**, human and machine contributions become continuously intertwined through prompting, evaluating and revising.

These arrangements can improve productivity, expand creative possibilities and enable new forms of work. However, automation complacency creates a risk that humans reduce oversight precisely because AI appears competent.

The book also explores AI's implications for creativity. When generating competent prose, images or ideas becomes inexpensive, human value increasingly depends on selecting, directing and judging outputs. Taste, originality and meaningful purpose remain consequential.

Education presents another opportunity and dilemma. AI can potentially provide personalised tutoring, explanations, practice and feedback at unprecedented scale. Yet automating beginner-level tasks raises a difficult question: how will people develop expertise if machines perform the work through which expertise traditionally emerges?

Mollick emphasises that experienced professionals are often better positioned to recognise AI mistakes and understand contextual limitations. Preserving and developing human capability therefore becomes an essential design problem.

The book closes with several possible trajectories for AI development, ranging from technological stagnation to transformative superintelligence. These are scenarios rather than predictions. Human institutions retain choices about how AI becomes integrated into everyday life.

**The central conclusion:** AI should be used actively as a powerful collaborator, with humans retaining responsibility for interpretation, verification and direction. The quality of co-intelligence depends on how people organise the partnership as the technology evolves.

items.title: Critical Thinking
items.author: Richard Paul & Linda Elder
items.summary:
Richard Paul and Linda Elder's *Critical Thinking* presents disciplined reasoning as a foundational capability for learning, judgment and everyday life. Their central argument is that people routinely think without adequately examining how their thoughts are formed. Because ordinary reasoning contains hidden assumptions, errors, prejudices and distortions, individuals must develop the capacity to analyse, evaluate and improve their own thinking.

The authors define critical thinking as self-directed, self-disciplined, self-monitored and self-corrective reasoning. It is a lifelong developmental practice rather than a technique used only for analysing arguments or detecting fallacies.

Their framework integrates **three essential dimensions: the elements of thought, intellectual standards and intellectual virtues**.

The elements of thought describe the underlying structure of reasoning. Every purposeful act of thinking involves a question, objective, information, interpretation, concepts, assumptions, implications and point of view. Making these components explicit enables individuals to examine the architecture of their judgments rather than accepting conclusions automatically.

Intellectual standards provide criteria for evaluating reasoning quality. Paul and Elder emphasise clarity, accuracy, precision, relevance, depth, breadth, logic, significance and fairness. These standards must be applied to the elements of thought. For example, evidence should be accurate and relevant, assumptions should be examined, and conclusions should follow logically from the available information.

The third dimension concerns intellectual character. The authors distinguish weak-sense critical thinking, in which analytical skill serves self-interest or manipulation, from strong-sense critical thinking, which applies demanding standards fairly to oneself and others.

Developing strong-sense critical thinking requires intellectual humility, courage, empathy, integrity, perseverance, autonomy and confidence in reason. These qualities enable individuals to examine uncomfortable evidence, consider opposing perspectives and revise deeply held beliefs.

Two persistent obstacles undermine this development.

**Egocentrism** describes the tendency to interpret experience through one's own desires, assumptions and interests while perceiving those interpretations as reasonable. People rationalise preferred conclusions, dismiss inconvenient evidence and resist challenges to self-image.

**Sociocentrism** extends similar distortions to groups. Cultural, professional, political and institutional affiliations can make shared assumptions appear self-evident. Critical thinking requires individuals to recognise these inherited perspectives and apply equivalent standards to their own groups and competing positions.

The authors apply their framework extensively to education. Genuine understanding involves learning how a discipline reasons, what questions it investigates, which concepts organise its knowledge and what constitutes acceptable evidence. Memorising information without understanding its intellectual structure produces inert knowledge that is difficult to apply.

The same methods extend to decision-making, ethical reasoning, media interpretation, problem-solving and evaluation of expert claims. Critical thinking becomes the way people approach intellectual activities rather than an additional activity performed separately.

Paul and Elder also describe six developmental stages: unreflective, challenged, beginning, practicing, advanced and master thinker. Progress involves growing awareness of one's reasoning weaknesses, sustained deliberate practice and the gradual integration of intellectual standards into habitual thought.

The authors emphasise that this development requires continuing effort. Knowledge of critical-thinking principles alone does not guarantee their application, particularly when emotions, identity or group loyalties are involved.

**The central conclusion:** Critical thinking is the disciplined practice of bringing one's own reasoning under examination. By analysing thought, applying intellectual standards, resisting personal and social distortion, and cultivating intellectual virtues, individuals progressively gain greater command over their learning, decisions and lives.

items.title: Damn Right!
items.author: Janet Lowe
items.summary:
Janet Lowe's *Damn Right!* examines the life and intellectual development of Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett's longtime business partner. The biography presents Munger's achievements as the cumulative result of character, self-education, disciplined reasoning, independent judgment and unusually selective decision-making. His investment wealth is an important outcome, but Lowe's broader subject is how he developed and applied a distinctive way of thinking and living.

Munger's early life established several enduring characteristics: thrift, independence, reliability, intellectual curiosity and a strong sense of personal responsibility. His Omaha upbringing emphasised hard work, ethical conduct and self-sufficiency. Books became a central source of education, allowing him to acquire knowledge well beyond his professional training.

Lowe also gives substantial attention to adversity. Munger experienced wartime disruption, divorce, severe personal financial setbacks, the death of his son Teddy and the loss of an eye following medical complications. These experiences complicate any straightforward narrative of uninterrupted success. They help explain his later emphasis on accepting reality, controlling emotional responses and addressing problems without self-pity.

A central theme is **the development of rational judgment through broad self-education**. Munger read across disciplines and valued fundamental explanations over superficial expertise. His interest in scientific reasoning encouraged an approach based on understanding underlying mechanisms, learning from mistakes and revising conclusions when evidence changed.

This intellectual discipline informed his investment method. Munger combined exceptional patience with occasional decisive action. Rather than continuously trading or pursuing marginal opportunities, he preferred to wait until an investment was understandable and the prospective reward justified significant commitment. He regarded unnecessary activity as a potential source of error.

The experience of Wheeler, Munger demonstrates both the benefits and difficulties of this approach. Although the partnership delivered impressive long-term returns, the severe market decline of 1973–1974 imposed substantial financial and psychological pressure. Munger ultimately chose to stop managing outside investors' money.

The acquisition of See's Candy became an important turning point in the investment philosophy shared by Munger and Buffett. It demonstrated the value of a durable franchise with loyal customers, pricing power and relatively modest capital requirements. The lesson was that a superior business purchased at a reasonable price could be more attractive than an apparently cheap business with weak economics.

Lowe portrays the Buffett–Munger partnership as a powerful combination of complementary strengths, mutual respect and intellectual honesty. Their capacity to disagree without personal hostility helped improve decisions.

Character remains inseparable from judgment. Integrity, responsibility, reputation and avoidance of ego are presented as practical advantages, not merely moral ideals. Wealth ultimately provided Munger with independence and opportunities for philanthropy, family support, institutional service and teaching.

**The central conclusion:** Munger's achievements resulted from the compounding effects of learning, character and disciplined judgment. Financial success created independence, but the deeper accomplishment was the freedom to think clearly, act selectively and contribute meaningfully.

items.title: Deaths of Despair and the Future of Capitalism
items.author: Anne Case & Angus Deaton
items.summary:
Anne Case and Angus Deaton investigate a disturbing reversal in American social progress: rising mortality among less-educated working-age Americans, particularly deaths associated with suicide, drug overdose and alcoholic liver disease. Their central argument is that these deaths are visible symptoms of a much broader deterioration in working-class life.

The authors identify a strong educational divide. Americans without four-year college degrees have experienced worsening mortality and health outcomes across successive generations, while college-educated Americans have generally followed more favourable trajectories. The crisis involves far more than the people who die. Chronic pain, disability, mental distress and declining wellbeing reveal extensive suffering beneath the mortality statistics.

The explanation begins with **the erosion of good work**. Stable employment historically provided wages, security, status, dignity and opportunities for social participation. It also supported marriage, family formation, community institutions and individual identity. As employment opportunities deteriorated, the consequences extended beyond household income.

Case and Deaton argue that the decline of working-class employment weakened the social foundations through which individuals construct meaningful lives. Economic insecurity, reduced bargaining power, precarious employment and disappearing career prospects contributed to declining family stability, social connection and perceived status.

The resulting mechanism cannot be reduced to lower wages directly producing suicide or addiction. Rather, deteriorating employment conditions interact with weakened social institutions, loss of dignity, chronic pain and psychological distress.

The opioid epidemic substantially amplified these conditions. Pharmaceutical companies aggressively promoted addictive medications, while regulatory and healthcare arrangements enabled widespread exposure. Opioids increased the lethality of existing vulnerabilities. The authors therefore treat the epidemic as an important accelerator of deaths of despair rather than their sole underlying cause.

A central question is why the United States experienced such pronounced deterioration when other wealthy countries also faced globalisation, technological change and industrial restructuring.

The authors argue that **American institutions magnified common economic pressures**. The erosion of organised labour weakened workers' bargaining power. Limited social protection increased exposure to insecurity. Market concentration and political influence facilitated the transfer of income toward powerful economic actors.

Healthcare receives particularly strong criticism. The United States devotes extraordinary resources to healthcare while achieving comparatively disappointing aggregate outcomes. High costs also affect employment, wages and public finances. Employer-funded healthcare increases labour costs and creates incentives that can discourage stable employment. The authors regard excessive pricing and protected market positions as important forms of rent-seeking.

Their criticism therefore concerns a particular organisation of capitalism. The problem is not simply economic inequality or capitalism as such, but institutions that allow concentrated economic and political power to extract value while undermining ordinary workers.

Case and Deaton favour reforms that restore competition, curb rent-seeking, strengthen labour-market institutions and address healthcare costs. Their objective is to improve the material and social conditions necessary for dignified lives.

**The central conclusion:** Deaths of despair reveal failures in American capitalism that extend far beyond mortality and income. Economic policy must restore the conditions for secure work, social participation, dignity and meaning while reducing institutional arrangements that privilege extraction over shared prosperity.

items.title: Do Social Norms Substitute for Enforcement?
items.author: Piskorski
items.summary:
*Do Social Norms Substitute for Enforcement? Evidence from Public Officials' Home Purchases in Singapore* examines whether strong social norms can eventually sustain ethical behaviour without continued formal enforcement. The paper addresses a fundamental institutional question: once a society establishes a reputation for integrity, can the resulting norms become sufficiently durable to replace some of the legal and administrative mechanisms that helped create them?

Singapore provides a particularly demanding empirical setting. Its strong public institutions and reputation for low corruption make it a plausible environment in which pro-integrity norms might become self-sustaining. If enforcement can eventually be relaxed without undermining compliance, such a setting should offer favourable conditions for observing that possibility.

The paper combines a dynamic conceptual model of norms and enforcement with detailed evidence concerning housing transactions by public officials and associated individuals.

The authors focus on residential property purchases near planned Mass Rapid Transit stations. Information about future MRT locations can materially affect property values. Officials with access to nonpublic planning information may therefore possess opportunities to gain financially through property purchases before information becomes publicly available.

The empirical analysis investigates whether purchasing behaviour is consistent with such informational advantages. It examines transaction timing, proximity to future station locations, institutional access, differences across official ranks and purchases by people associated with public officials.

The results indicate patterns consistent with informed purchasing before the tightening of enforcement arrangements in 2011–2012. The authors find that the behaviour is particularly concentrated among certain middle-ranking officials, with related patterns involving individuals registered at the same residential address.

These findings require careful interpretation. The researchers do not directly observe officials receiving confidential information, nor do they establish every purchaser's motivation. Their inference rests on the combined evidence from timing, spatial patterns, institutional proximity and additional tests intended to distinguish privileged information from ordinary investment behaviour.

The subsequent enforcement tightening provides an important opportunity to examine behavioural responses. Purchasing patterns consistent with exploitation of nonpublic information decline significantly afterward.

The theoretical mechanism involves a relationship between **formal deterrence and informal norms**. Enforcement raises the expected cost of misconduct directly. It can also influence the value individuals place on maintaining an honest reputation and complying with prevailing expectations.

The paper's findings are more consistent with limited persistence of pro-integrity norms than with an equilibrium in which strong norms independently sustain compliance. The authors also use survey evidence concerning attitudes toward corruption and institutional trust, while recognising that such measures are imperfect indicators of actual behaviour.

The interpretation is deliberately qualified. The enforcement episode involved several institutional developments rather than a single isolated policy intervention. The precise persistence of norms is inferred rather than directly estimated.

The study also illustrates a broader methodological point: high institutional integrity and favourable public attitudes cannot establish the absence of hidden misconduct. Administrative and transaction-level evidence may reveal behaviour that survey responses cannot detect.

**The central conclusion:** Strong integrity norms remain valuable, but they may depend on continued credible enforcement. Even successful anti-corruption systems cannot safely assume that formal deterrence has become unnecessary merely because compliance appears well established.

items.title: Dooyeweerd's Philosophy
items.author: Andrew Basden
items.summary:
Andrew Basden's examination of Herman Dooyeweerd's philosophy explores how philosophical concepts can improve the conduct and interpretation of research. His central argument is that research should be understood as a responsible human activity embedded within everyday reality, rather than as theoretically detached reasoning conducted independently of social, practical and ethical contexts.

Basden draws on Dooyeweerd's emphasis on meaningfulness, diversity, coherence and the limits of theoretical thought. The resulting perspective challenges reductionist approaches that privilege one explanatory dimension while neglecting other important aspects of reality.

A foundational proposition is that **everyday experience provides a necessary starting point for research**. Human activities exist within complex settings involving physical, biological, psychological, social, economic, legal and ethical dimensions. Theoretical analysis isolates selected features to make investigation possible, but this necessary abstraction can obscure relationships that remain important to the phenomenon being studied.

Dooyeweerd's theory of modal aspects provides a systematic means of recognising diversity within reality. The framework identifies fifteen distinguishable aspects of meaningfulness, each associated with a different mode of functioning and normativity.

Basden treats these aspects as analytical tools rather than isolated categories to memorise. Their value lies in encouraging researchers to ask which dimensions their methods illuminate, which are neglected and how the different aspects interact.

This provides an alternative to disciplinary reductionism. A technological system, for example, cannot be understood adequately through technical efficiency alone. Its economic effects, social relationships, communicative practices, legal responsibilities and ethical consequences may be equally important.

The framework also helps clarify disagreements among research paradigms. Different intellectual traditions may concentrate on different aspects of the same underlying reality. Recognising these partial viewpoints creates opportunities for dialogue while revealing the limitations of claims to comprehensive explanation.

Basden further examines the **non-neutrality of theoretical thought**. Research depends on assumptions about what constitutes knowledge, which questions matter and which forms of evidence count. These assumptions may reflect deeper philosophical commitments that are rarely made explicit.

Dooyeweerd's Christian intellectual origins are important to this discussion, particularly his treatment of religious ground-motives and the origin of meaningfulness. Basden nevertheless invites researchers from different commitments to investigate the framework critically rather than requiring prior acceptance of its religious foundations.

The book moves from philosophical foundations toward research practice. Aspectual analysis can inform literature reviews, conceptual frameworks, research design, data collection, interpretation and evaluation. It can also help researchers consider the broader repercussions of their findings and applications.

Basden acknowledges that practical usefulness does not establish philosophical correctness. He examines criticisms and limitations, encouraging adaptation, further testing and rejection where the framework proves inadequate.

This provisional stance is essential. Dooyeweerd's philosophy is presented as a potentially fruitful resource for interdisciplinary inquiry rather than a complete solution to every research problem.

**The central conclusion:** More responsible research requires theoretical precision alongside sensitivity to the many dimensions of everyday reality. Dooyeweerd's philosophy offers tools for achieving that balance, but their worth must be established through critical use and continued examination.

items.title: Fixed: Why Personal Finance Is Broken and How to Make It Work for Everyone
items.author: John Y. Campbell & Tarun Ramadorai
items.summary:
John Campbell and Tarun Ramadorai argue that contemporary personal finance places excessive demands on ordinary households while frequently rewarding financial institutions for complexity, opacity and poorly understood costs.

Their book uses the word *fixed* in two senses. The system is effectively fixed against many consumers because its design advantages sophisticated participants and providers. It also needs to be fixed through deliberate institutional reform.

The authors begin with the mismatch between human decision-making and financial complexity. Households must make consequential choices about borrowing, saving, insurance, housing, investment and retirement, often without specialist knowledge. These decisions involve uncertainty, long time horizons, unfamiliar terminology and difficult comparisons between products.

Behavioural limitations make the challenge more severe. Individuals may misunderstand compounding, discount distant consequences, underestimate risk, focus on misleading headline prices or fail to compare alternatives adequately.

Financial institutions can benefit from these mistakes. Complex fees, opaque pricing, poorly structured incentives and aggressive product design may transfer value from consumers to providers. Even competitive markets do not necessarily correct these problems when customers cannot evaluate products effectively.

The authors explore financial decisions across the household life cycle.

Borrowing and consumption-smoothing products can help households manage income fluctuations, yet inappropriate loan structures and poorly understood costs can create debt traps.

Housing is both an essential consumption good and a large, leveraged investment. Mortgage choices expose households to interest-rate, refinancing and liquidity risks that are difficult to evaluate.

Insurance can protect households against major financial shocks, but coverage decisions are complicated by exclusions, product design and uncertainty about future needs.

Retirement saving poses particularly demanding problems because individuals must plan across decades, evaluate investment risk and manage the possibility of living longer than expected.

Financial technology can reduce transaction costs and improve access to information. However, greater technological sophistication does not automatically make products safer or consumer decisions better. Digital interfaces can also amplify behavioural vulnerabilities or increase the speed at which costly mistakes occur.

The authors' principal recommendation is a more interventionist approach to consumer financial protection. They argue for moving beyond traditional disclosure requirements, financial education and behavioural nudges toward a stronger governmental **shove** that reshapes market architecture.

Their preferred system emphasises four product-design principles: **simple, cheap, safe and easy**.

They propose a standardised starter kit of financial products suitable for ordinary consumers. Such products should provide understandable, low-cost foundations for essential financial needs while allowing individuals to adopt more sophisticated arrangements as their experience and requirements develop.

This approach does not imply uniform financial products for every household. The authors recognise differences in national institutions, household circumstances and financial capability. The objective is to create a dependable default architecture while preserving appropriate choice.

The broader claim is that better outcomes require changing the financial environment rather than assuming consumers can individually overcome every structural disadvantage.

**The central conclusion:** Personal finance is too important to depend on households becoming financial experts. Governments should redesign the system so that essential financial decisions are supported by products and institutions that are simple, inexpensive, safe and genuinely usable.

items.title: Government in Business
items.author: Lim Hwee Hua
items.summary:
Lim Hwee Hua's *Government in Business* examines the appropriate relationship between the state and commercial enterprise. Its central argument is that government participation in business cannot be judged through a fixed ideological preference for either state ownership or private markets. The legitimacy and effectiveness of intervention depend on circumstances, institutional competence and the ability to change direction as economic conditions evolve.

Government involvement may be justified by market failures, the provision of public goods, infrastructure requirements, strategic capability development or extraordinary crises. Yet the original reasons for intervention may weaken as markets and institutions mature. A government that enters for legitimate reasons must therefore remain capable of reassessing whether it should continue, change its role or withdraw.

The book proposes a **dynamic decision framework** based on four considerations: the state of the economy, the state of government, the state of the market and the appropriate mode of engagement.

The state of the economy determines the problems requiring attention. A developing economy facing inadequate infrastructure or limited private capital may justify a different form of intervention from an advanced economy with sophisticated commercial institutions.

The state of government matters because intervention requires resources, expertise, fiscal capacity and credible institutions. Even a theoretically justified policy can produce poor outcomes when the state lacks the capabilities necessary to implement it.

The state of the market determines whether private enterprise can already provide the relevant goods and services effectively. Intervention becomes harder to justify when functioning markets can deliver suitable outcomes without sustained state participation.

The mode of engagement concerns the means chosen. Government can influence markets through regulation, taxation, incentives, partnerships, procurement, financing or direct ownership. These instruments differ substantially in their implications for accountability, incentives, competition and risk.

A central distinction is therefore between **government responsibility and government ownership**. The state may have legitimate reasons to ensure an outcome without needing to produce that outcome through a government-owned enterprise.

Lim also addresses governance problems created when government simultaneously acts as policymaker, regulator and shareholder. Conflicting roles can produce moral hazard, distort competition or create uncertainty about the objectives of public enterprises. Clear institutional separation and professional governance help reduce these risks.

Government involvement can create confidence and stability, particularly during crises, but excessive intervention may weaken private initiative or delay necessary restructuring. Public authorities must therefore preserve flexibility and avoid treating temporary arrangements as permanent institutional commitments.

Singapore's development experience provides an important context for the discussion, illustrating how public participation and market orientation can coexist. However, the book resists assuming that one country's institutional arrangements can simply be transferred unchanged to another.

Its broader emphasis is on **entry, adaptation and exit**. Effective government must remain attentive to the changing relationship between public objectives and private capabilities. Intervention should be evaluated through evidence of continuing need and performance rather than defended solely through history or ideology.

**The central conclusion:** Government can be a productive partner to business when its intervention is justified, competently governed and responsive to changing conditions. The best institutional arrangement is one that combines market orientation, sensitivity to society's needs and the capacity for continuous adjustment.

items.title: Hayek's Bastards
items.author: Quinn Slobodian
items.summary:
Quinn Slobodian's *Hayek's Bastards* investigates the intellectual connections between neoliberalism and the contemporary populist right. His central argument challenges the familiar interpretation of right-wing populism as a straightforward rebellion against neoliberal economic ideology. Instead, he traces important strands of contemporary nationalist and exclusionary politics to debates and transformations occurring within neoliberal intellectual traditions themselves.

Neoliberalism is often associated with free markets, international economic integration, limited government and individual liberty. Slobodian argues that this representation overlooks the diversity of political arrangements developed by thinkers committed to protecting capitalism from democratic intervention.

A recurring neoliberal concern was how to defend market institutions against political majorities demanding redistribution, regulation or greater economic equality. Different thinkers proposed different institutional safeguards, including constitutional restrictions, supranational protections, strong property rights and limits on democratic authority.

Slobodian examines how one branch of this intellectual tradition increasingly connected market liberalism to arguments about culture, national identity, inherited characteristics and social hierarchy.

The resulting politics combined commitments to private property and market competition with exclusionary understandings of political membership.

**The central continuity is the defence of capitalist order.** The point of divergence concerns which populations, institutions and political communities should be trusted to sustain that order.

Slobodian traces debates involving cultural evolution, heredity and the perceived foundations of economic behaviour. Some thinkers came to interpret differences in institutional success through supposedly persistent cultural or biological characteristics. These arguments provided intellectual resources for political programmes that defend market freedom while restricting social inclusion.

The book also examines sovereignist and secessionist ideas. Rather than treating global economic integration as the only possible institutional solution, certain market-oriented thinkers favoured smaller political units, cultural homogeneity or forms of national sovereignty intended to protect preferred economic arrangements.

Contemporary right-wing figures and movements illustrate how these traditions entered practical politics. Slobodian examines the combination of market-oriented economic commitments, hostility to egalitarian redistribution and increasingly explicit nationalist or exclusionary positions.

These political formations are not intellectually identical. The book does not argue that all neoliberalism inevitably produces the far right. Its historical claim is more specific: important exclusionary tendencies existed within parts of neoliberal thought and became increasingly influential under changing political conditions.

This interpretation also challenges a simple opposition between globalism and nationalism. Both can serve projects aimed at preserving capitalism while limiting democratic demands on property and markets.

The book's genealogical approach is particularly important. Slobodian reconstructs intellectual relationships, institutional networks and political adaptations rather than claiming that contemporary populists merely repeat the programmes of earlier economists.

The implications extend to current debates about economic liberalism, democracy and political belonging. Market freedom can coexist with restrictions on participation, social solidarity and political equality. The meaning of liberty therefore depends partly on who is included in the political community and which institutions receive protection.

**The central conclusion:** Significant strands of contemporary right-wing populism emerged through transformations within neoliberal traditions. Their combination of market liberalism with nationalism and exclusionary ideas reflects an internal political possibility of neoliberalism rather than simply its ideological rejection.

items.title: How to Survive the AI Shock
items.author: Robinson et al.
items.summary:
*How to Survive the AI Shock* examines the political and economic consequences of rapid artificial-intelligence adoption. Its central argument is that AI offers potentially substantial productivity gains while creating unusually concentrated labour-market disruption. Without credible mechanisms to support displaced workers, political resistance could slow adoption and undermine the economic benefits the technology might otherwise deliver.

The authors frame AI as a powerful engine of creative destruction. Technological progress raises productivity by reorganising production and replacing some existing activities. Historically, such changes have produced aggregate economic gains while imposing substantial costs on particular workers, industries and communities.

AI may intensify this problem because its capabilities apply to many cognitive occupations and can improve rapidly. Workers may face displacement before existing training systems, employers or labour-market institutions can provide realistic alternatives.

The resulting problem is partly one of timing. Productivity benefits may emerge across the economy over many years, while employment losses are immediate and concentrated. People experiencing displacement cannot necessarily wait for the long-term benefits of technological adjustment.

The authors emphasise the weaknesses of existing American labour-market institutions. Retraining programmes may be difficult to access, poorly aligned with employment opportunities or insufficiently responsive to technological change. Workers moving into new occupations may also suffer permanent reductions in earnings.

**The political consequence is central to the argument.** Concentrated losses can generate opposition to technological adoption even when aggregate gains are substantial. Public pressure may lead governments to restrict AI deployment, introduce protective regulations or otherwise slow the diffusion of productivity-enhancing technology.

The authors therefore propose a policy bargain intended to preserve both innovation and social consent.

First, they recommend **portable retraining tax credits**. Workers should be able to obtain support for acquiring skills suited to changing employment opportunities. Portability reduces dependence on a particular employer, while tax-based support gives individuals more flexibility than narrowly prescribed training programmes.

Second, they advocate **wage-loss insurance**. Workers displaced into lower-paying employment would receive temporary financial support reflecting part of their lost earnings. The mechanism is intended to make reemployment more attractive and reduce the economic shock associated with occupational transitions.

Third, they propose financing these measures through a **payroll tax on equity compensation**. The rationale is that equity-linked remuneration is one channel through which gains from technological innovation accrue to highly compensated individuals. Using part of these gains to finance adjustment support creates a connection between technological benefits and the costs of transition.

The programme is designed to address adjustment directly rather than to prevent automation. Its purpose is to help people move toward new employment opportunities instead of preserving every existing job.

The authors also argue against excessive reliance on government predictions about which occupations will grow. Technological change is difficult to forecast, and training mechanisms should allow flexibility as labour demand evolves.

The proposal is specifically situated in the American political and institutional context. Its details should therefore be understood as a policy design rather than a universal formula for every economy.

**The central conclusion:** AI's productivity promise and political risks arise from the same process of rapid economic transformation. Early, credible support for displaced workers can reduce backlash while preserving the conditions for innovation and long-term growth.

items.title: How to Teach Critical Thinking
items.author: Daniel T. Willingham
items.summary:
On closer inspection, the merged export does contain a substantive Blueprint for this paper. This replaces the earlier skipped entry.

Daniel T. Willingham's *How to Teach Critical Thinking* examines how educators can develop students' reasoning capabilities when skills learned in one context often fail to transfer reliably to another.

Its central argument is that critical thinking can be taught, but effective instruction depends heavily on domain-specific knowledge, explicitly taught strategies and sustained practice.

Willingham challenges the assumption that students can acquire a single general-purpose thinking skill and subsequently apply it across unrelated subjects.

The problem is **transfer**.

A student who successfully evaluates evidence in one discipline may struggle with apparently similar reasoning in another because the relevant knowledge, conventions and problem structures differ.

Critical thinking therefore cannot be separated easily from what a person knows about the subject being considered.

**Domain knowledge supports reasoning in several ways.**

It helps individuals recognise meaningful patterns, distinguish relevant from irrelevant information and identify which strategies are appropriate.

Knowledge stored in long-term memory also reduces demands on working memory, allowing greater attention to complex reasoning.

Without sufficient background knowledge, individuals may understand general advice about evaluating arguments while remaining unable to apply it effectively.

The paper also distinguishes several characteristics of critical thinking, including novelty, self-direction and effectiveness.

The standards for effective thinking depend partly on the intellectual domain. Historical interpretation, scientific experimentation and mathematical proof require different types of evidence and reasoning.

Willingham therefore advocates explicit instruction in the thinking practices relevant to particular subjects.

Rather than merely encouraging students to think critically, teachers should identify the specific intellectual activities they want students to master.

These activities should then be connected to the knowledge necessary for successful performance.

The Blueprint identifies a practical curriculum approach involving four stages.

First, **identify the particular thinking skills** required within a discipline.

Second, **select the relevant domain knowledge** needed to apply those skills.

Third, **sequence instruction** so that students develop the necessary foundations before encountering more demanding problems.

Fourth, **revisit and practise** these forms of thinking across multiple years, allowing competence to become more robust.

Practice should include varied examples and opportunities to recognise when particular strategies apply.

The paper's argument is pragmatic rather than absolute. Willingham does not prove that domain-general critical-thinking abilities cannot exist. His position is that research provides a stronger foundation for teaching specific forms of reasoning supported by relevant knowledge.

This has important implications for curriculum design.

Critical thinking should be developed through sustained disciplinary learning rather than treated as an isolated educational programme.

**The central conclusion:** Critical thinking improves when educators teach specific reasoning practices together with the knowledge that makes those practices effective. Durable capability requires explicit instruction, careful sequencing and repeated practice across meaningful contexts.

items.title: Human Compatible
items.author: Stuart Russell
items.summary:
Stuart Russell's *Human Compatible* examines how increasingly powerful artificial intelligence can remain beneficial to humanity. His central argument is that the conventional foundations of AI contain a dangerous assumption: machines should be designed to optimise objectives specified by humans.

This approach becomes problematic because human beings cannot perfectly specify everything they value. A machine may perform extremely well against its programmed objective while producing outcomes that its designers never intended. As capability increases, even small specification errors can become consequential.

Russell argues that the problem is structural. Powerful optimising agents may develop instrumental incentives to acquire resources, preserve their objectives and resist interference. These behaviours can arise regardless of whether their ultimate goals resemble ordinary human ambitions.

The familiar assumption that greater intelligence naturally produces better moral judgment is therefore unreliable. A system can be extremely capable at achieving objectives that are incompatible with human wellbeing.

Russell proposes replacing this conventional model with **beneficial AI**, based on three principles. The machine's objective should be to maximise the realisation of human preferences. It should initially remain uncertain about those preferences. Human behaviour should provide evidence from which the machine can learn what people prefer.
